title: Terraform Modules & Multi-Environment Structure
summary: Structuring Terraform so dev, stage, and prod don't mean copy-pasted, drifting code.

slides.subTitle: Inputs, outputs, composition
slides.markdown:
A **module** is just a directory of `.tf` files with defined **inputs** (`variable` blocks) and **outputs** (`output` blocks) — a reusable unit, the same idea as a function in a programming language. A "networking" module might take `cidr_block` and `az_count` as input and output a list of subnet IDs; any config that calls it gets a VPC without re-writing VPC logic.

**Composition** means building bigger infrastructure from smaller modules — a "web-app" module that internally calls the "networking" module and a "compute" module, rather than one flat file describing everything.

The **root module** is whatever directory you run `terraform apply` from — every Terraform config has exactly one, even if it's tiny. A **child module** is called from the root (or from another module) via a `module` block and receives its inputs explicitly: `module "vpc" { source = "./modules/vpc"; cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/16" }`.

A child module has no implicit access to the root's variables or state beyond what's explicitly passed in — this explicitness is what makes a well-written module safely reusable across completely different projects.

Two ways to keep dev/stage/prod state from colliding.

| | Workspaces | Separate state files per environment |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | One config, `terraform workspace select prod` switches state | One backend config (or directory) per environment, explicitly |
| Isolation | Same backend, same code path — easy to typo the wrong workspace | Physically separate, harder to touch the wrong one by accident |
| Common use | Short-lived, similar environments (feature-branch previews) | Long-lived environments with real differences (prod vs dev) |

Most teams use separate state (and often separate variable files, per the worked example) for dev/stage/prod specifically because the blast radius of an accidental cross-environment apply is too high for workspace-switching to feel safe.

slides.subTitle: One module, three environments

slides.markdown:
A module `source` can point at a git ref or a registry version: `source = "git::https://example.com/modules.git//vpc?ref=v2.1.0"`. Pinning to a specific tag means every environment calling that module gets the **exact same, reviewed** version — an unpinned reference to a branch means the module's behavior can silently change under you the next time someone runs `init` or `get`.

Bumping a module version deliberately (updating the `ref`) and reviewing the diff is the same discipline as bumping any other dependency — treat a shared internal module the same as a third-party library.

slides.subTitle: One giant root module
slides.markdown:
**The wrong belief:** "one big root module for dev, staging, and prod together keeps everything consistent."

**Why it breaks:** every `apply` touches every environment's resources at once — a prod-only mistake can be applied alongside dev changes in one command, and the **blast radius** of any error is the entire fleet, not one environment.

**The correct model:** separate root modules per environment, sharing logic through **child modules** — consistency comes from reused code, not a shared blast radius.
